How to Determine Your Hourly Wage in Texas

To determine your hourly wage, divide the compensation you receive by the number of hours you work during the same period. For a standard full-time salary, divide the annual salary by 2,080 hours, based on 40 hours per week for 52 weeks.

However, that simple calculation does not always determine the hourly rate used for minimum wage or overtime purposes. Bonuses, commissions, tips, multiple pay rates, and actual hours worked may affect the calculation.

What Is an Hourly Wage?

An hourly wage is the amount an employee earns for each hour worked.

For an employee paid directly by the hour, the rate may be clearly stated on a pay stub or employment agreement. For a salaried, commissioned, or piece-rate employee, determining the effective hourly wage may require an additional calculation.

Understanding your hourly wage can help you:

  • Compare job offers
  • Review your paycheck
  • Estimate overtime pay
  • Calculate lost wages
  • Identify possible underpayment
  • Understand the value of your working time

How Do You Determine an Hourly Wage From an Annual Salary?

A common salary-to-hourly formula is:

Annual salary ÷ annual work hours = estimated hourly wage

A standard full-time schedule is commonly calculated as:

40 hours per week × 52 weeks = 2,080 hours per year

Therefore, an employee earning $52,000 per year would calculate the estimated hourly rate as follows:

$52,000 ÷ 2,080 = $25 per hour

This calculation is useful for comparing compensation, but it may not be the correct legal calculation for every overtime situation.

What Is the Hourly Wage for Common Annual Salaries?

Annual Salary Approximate Hourly Wage
$30,000 $14.42
$40,000 $19.23
$50,000 $24.04
$60,000 $28.85
$75,000 $36.06
$80,000 $38.46
$100,000 $48.08
$125,000 $60.10

These estimates assume a 40-hour workweek and 52 paid weeks per year.

How Do You Determine Your Hourly Wage From Weekly Pay?

Divide your gross weekly compensation by the number of hours worked during that week.

For example, an employee who earns $800 for 40 hours of work has an hourly wage of:

$800 ÷ 40 = $20 per hour

If the same employee works 50 hours for the same $800 salary, the simple effective hourly rate would be:

$800 ÷ 50 = $16 per hour

That does not necessarily mean $16 is the employee’s correct legal overtime rate. The Fair Labor Standards Act may require a different calculation depending on the compensation arrangement and exemption status.

How Do You Determine Your Hourly Wage From a Paycheck?

Start with the gross pay listed on the paycheck, not the amount received after taxes and deductions.

Then divide the gross compensation by the hours covered by that paycheck.

For example:

  • Gross weekly pay: $900
  • Hours worked: 40
  • Estimated hourly wage: $22.50

Gross pay represents compensation before deductions for taxes, health insurance, retirement contributions, or other authorized amounts.

What Is the Difference Between Gross and Net Hourly Pay?

Gross hourly pay is the amount earned before deductions. Net hourly pay is the amount remaining after deductions.

For example, an employee may earn a gross rate of $25 per hour but receive a lower net amount after:

  • Federal income tax withholding
  • Social Security and Medicare taxes
  • Health insurance premiums
  • Retirement contributions
  • Other authorized deductions

Wage and overtime calculations generally begin with gross compensation rather than take-home pay.

What Is the Minimum Hourly Wage in Texas?

Texas adopts the federal minimum wage. In 2026, the applicable minimum wage remains $7.25 per hour for covered non-exempt employees.

Some workers and employers may be subject to exceptions or special rules. Tipped employees, certain students, and workers in specific occupations may be governed by different requirements.

An employment agreement may also provide a rate higher than the legal minimum.

Does Being Paid a Salary Eliminate Overtime Rights?

No. Receiving a salary does not automatically make an employee exempt from overtime.

Overtime eligibility generally depends on factors such as:

  • The employee’s actual job duties
  • The applicable legal exemption
  • The method and amount of compensation
  • The employer’s and employee’s coverage under the law

A job title alone does not determine whether an employee is exempt.

How Is Overtime Pay Determined?

Covered non-exempt employees are generally entitled to overtime compensation for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.

The usual overtime rate is at least one and one-half times the employee’s regular rate of pay.

For example, an employee with a regular rate of $20 per hour would generally have an overtime rate of:

$20 × 1.5 = $30 per hour

If that employee works 45 hours, the basic calculation would be:

  • 40 regular hours × $20 = $800
  • 5 overtime hours × $30 = $150
  • Total gross weekly pay = $950

Is the Regular Rate the Same as the Hourly Rate?

Not always.

The regular rate is a legal calculation used to determine overtime compensation. It may include more than the employee’s stated hourly wage.

For many non-exempt employees, the regular rate is calculated by dividing total includable compensation for the workweek by the total hours worked.

Depending on the circumstances, compensation included in the regular rate may involve:

  • Hourly wages
  • Salary payments
  • Commissions
  • Production incentives
  • Certain nondiscretionary bonuses
  • Shift differentials

Certain payments may legally be excluded. The label an employer gives a payment does not always determine whether it must be included.

How Do Bonuses Affect an Hourly Wage?

Certain nondiscretionary bonuses may need to be included in the regular rate used for overtime calculations.

A nondiscretionary bonus is commonly tied to predetermined standards such as:

  • Attendance
  • Productivity
  • Sales goals
  • Quality targets
  • Individual or team performance

A truly discretionary bonus may receive different treatment. The specific terms and circumstances of the payment matter.

How Do Commissions Affect the Hourly Rate?

Commission-based compensation may affect an employee’s regular rate.

When commissions are included in compensation for a workweek, the employer may need to allocate them correctly when calculating overtime.

Commission employees are not automatically exempt from overtime simply because they earn commissions.

Eligibility depends on the employee’s duties, industry, compensation structure, and any applicable exemption.

How Do Multiple Pay Rates Affect Overtime?

An employee may perform different jobs at different hourly rates during the same workweek.

In many situations, the regular rate is determined using a weighted average of the different rates.

For example, suppose an employee works:

  • 30 hours at $20 per hour
  • 10 hours at $15 per hour

The total straight-time compensation is $750. Dividing that amount by 40 hours produces a weighted average rate of $18.75 per hour.

If overtime is worked, the appropriate overtime calculation may be based on that regular rate unless another lawful method applies.

Should Paid Time Off Be Included in Hours Worked?

Usually, paid vacation, holidays, or sick leave do not count as hours worked when determining whether an employee exceeded 40 working hours under the FLSA.

For example, an employee who performs 32 hours of work and receives eight hours of holiday pay may receive compensation for 40 hours without having worked overtime.

Employer policies or employment agreements may provide more generous benefits.

Does Weekend or Holiday Work Automatically Receive Overtime?

No. Federal law generally does not require additional pay merely because work occurs on a Saturday, Sunday, holiday, or night.

Overtime generally depends on whether a covered non-exempt employee works more than 40 hours during the employer’s established workweek.

An employment contract, collective bargaining agreement, or company policy may provide premium pay for those shifts.

What Hours Must Be Included in the Calculation?

Employers generally must count compensable working time, even when that work occurs outside the employee’s scheduled shift.

Potential examples include:

  • Completing required tasks before clocking in
  • Cleaning or closing after clocking out
  • Responding to required work messages
  • Attending mandatory meetings
  • Completing required training
  • Working through automatically deducted meal periods

Accurately determining an hourly wage or overtime amount requires an accurate record of all compensable hours worked.

What Are Common Hourly Wage Calculation Errors?

Common wage calculation problems include:

  • Dividing annual salary by the wrong number of hours
  • Failing to count off-the-clock work
  • Assuming every salaried employee is exempt
  • Leaving commissions out of the regular rate
  • Excluding nondiscretionary bonuses
  • Using the stated hourly rate instead of the correct regular rate
  • Failing to apply a weighted average for multiple rates
  • Calculating overtime from the wrong base rate
  • Making deductions that reduce pay below minimum wage

How Can Employees Check Whether They Were Paid Correctly?

Employees should compare their pay records with the hours they actually worked.

Useful documentation may include:

  • Pay stubs
  • Timesheets
  • Schedules
  • Employment agreements
  • Bonus and commission plans
  • Emails and work messages
  • Personal records of hours worked

An employee should also review whether all regular wages, overtime, bonuses, and commissions were included correctly.

What Can You Do If Your Hourly Wage Was Calculated Incorrectly?

An employee who believes wages were underpaid may have options under federal or Texas law.

Depending on the circumstances, potential options may include:

  • Requesting payroll records
  • Reporting the issue internally
  • Filing a wage claim with the Texas Workforce Commission
  • Contacting the U.S. Department of Labor
  • Evaluating a claim for unpaid wages or overtime

Deadlines may apply, so employees should avoid waiting indefinitely to review suspected underpayment.

Can an Employer Retaliate Against You for Questioning Your Pay?

Employers generally cannot lawfully retaliate against employees for asserting protected wage rights.

Possible retaliation may include:

  • Termination
  • Reduced hours
  • Demotion
  • Discipline
  • Unfavorable assignments
  • Threats or harassment

Employees should preserve documentation showing when they raised the wage issue and what happened afterward.

How The Lange Firm Helps Houston and Texas Employees

The Lange Firm helps employees in Houston and throughout Texas evaluate employment matters involving:

  • Unpaid wages
  • Unpaid overtime
  • Employee misclassification
  • Commission disputes
  • Off-the-clock work
  • Minimum wage violations
  • Workplace retaliation

Determining the correct hourly wage is often the first step in identifying whether an employee received all compensation legally owed.

Frequently Asked Questions About Determining Hourly Wage

How do I determine my hourly wage from salary?

Divide your annual salary by the number of hours you are expected to work annually. A common estimate uses 2,080 hours for a 40-hour workweek over 52 weeks.

What is the hourly wage for a $52,000 salary?

A $52,000 annual salary divided by 2,080 hours equals approximately $25 per hour.

Does salary mean I am not entitled to overtime?

No. Salary status alone does not determine overtime eligibility. Actual job duties, compensation, coverage, and applicable exemptions must be considered.

Are bonuses included when determining the overtime rate?

Certain nondiscretionary bonuses must generally be included in the regular rate used to calculate overtime. Truly discretionary bonuses may be treated differently.

What should I do if my employer calculated my wage incorrectly?

Preserve pay records and working-time evidence, review the calculation, and consider seeking guidance about available wage claim options and filing deadlines.

Conclusion

Determining an hourly wage may be as simple as dividing compensation by hours worked, but legal wage calculations can involve additional rules.

Bonuses, commissions, multiple pay rates, overtime, and uncompensated working time can all affect what an employee should have received.

  • Divide annual salary by 2,080 for a basic full-time hourly estimate.
  • Do not assume that receiving a salary eliminates overtime rights.
  • The regular rate may include commissions, shift differentials, and certain bonuses.

Employees who understand their hourly rate are better positioned to compare compensation, identify errors, and determine whether wages may be unpaid.
